passage: The class fish tank was leaking onto the shelf, and the teacher's eyes landed on Leela. "You were the last one near it at break." Leela's ears burned, but she did not shout. "I was filling my water bottle at the tap," she said. "The lid was already cracked when I walked past. Please look at it again." The teacher paused and said they would think about it. By the door, Trisha stared at her shoes. She had leaned on that lid while reaching for her pencil case, and her throat had locked when the teacher's voice rose. Her stomach had felt sick ever since. Leela saw her friend's face and understood. At home she told her father, Hemant, everything, and her voice shook more than it had in class. He listened and offered to help her write a short note to the teacher. Leela did not speak to Trisha for two days. On the third morning, Trisha walked up in the corridor, pale, and said, "I have to tell the teacher it was me. Will you come with me?" Leela looked at her for a long moment before she answered.

qa.q: What was leaking onto the shelf?
qa.a: The class fish tank was leaking onto the shelf.

qa.q: How did Leela's way of facing the blame differ from what Trisha did at first, and what did Trisha choose three days later?
qa.a: Leela explained with facts and asked the teacher to look again, while Trisha stayed silent and stared at her shoes because she was scared; on the third morning Trisha chose to go and tell the teacher the truth.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she saw Trisha's face by the door?
qa.a: She felt hurt and let down, because she understood her friend had done it and let her take the blame; she stayed quiet with Trisha for two days while she decided what to do.

qa.q: What could Trisha do after telling the teacher to help mend things with Leela?
qa.a: She could apologise to Leela and say plainly that she was scared, then give Leela time to decide slowly whether to trust her again.

grounding: One classroom accident is seen by the girl blamed, the friend who stayed silent out of fear, and a parent who helps, showing how each stance leads to different actions.

passage: Thursday in the college lab, Samir's juniors crowded around his laptop again. "Your code never breaks," one said. Samir laughed and scrolled to the version that had crashed three times last week. "Look at this mess. I just don't show it." Across the room his classmate Shalini, who had barely spoken to him all term, turned her chair away when he greeted her. He went over recent weeks in his head once: no quarrel, no favour left unreturned. He shrugged and stopped waving at her. That evening he posted the club's result on a public page, and by midnight strangers were mocking his photo and the team. He did not answer a single one. He saved the worst comments in a folder, blocked the accounts, and phoned his roommate, who told him to come and eat. Harish, who sat beside him in class and had beaten him in every test, passed over a marked paper with a higher score. Samir felt his jaw tighten, then asked how Harish had solved the last question. He copied the method into his notebook, and next week he lent Harish his spare charger when the lab socket failed.

qa.q: What did Samir save in a folder?
qa.a: He saved the worst comments in a folder.

qa.q: How did Samir's response to the strangers online differ from his response to Shalini turning her chair away?
qa.a: With the strangers he did not answer, saved the comments, blocked the accounts and leaned on his roommate; with Shalini he thought once about whether he had done wrong and then stopped waving at her, so in neither case did he keep chasing approval.

qa.q: How was Samir feeling when Harish passed him the paper with the higher score?
qa.a: His jaw tightened, so he felt stung and a little envious, but he turned that into curiosity about Harish's method.

qa.q: What could Samir keep doing so his juniors' praise does not inflate him?
qa.a: He can keep showing them his crashed versions and admitting his flaws, as he did when he scrolled to the messy code. 🙂

grounding: One student meets admiration from juniors, dislike from a classmate, an online pile-on and a constant rival, and handles each in a different wise way.

passage: At the vegetable market Jomon spotted a jar of orange sweets and asked for one. "Not today," said his father, Naveen, calmly. Jomon's face crumpled. He screamed, dropped flat on the wet floor and kicked off his sandals. His body felt huge and hot. Naveen crouched beside him, kept his voice low and said, "We are not buying sweets. Breathe with me. In, and out." Jomon gulped air until the screaming shrank to hiccups. Then he saw people watching and hid his face in his father's shirt. "You were upset, it's done now, and we'll sort out your sandals together," Naveen said, and they did. Next morning at school, Ujjwal threw his crayon box and shrieked when a puzzle piece would not fit. Jomon's tummy went tight. He backed away to the shelf, unsure what to do, then walked to the teacher and said, "Ujjwal is really loud." The teacher went to him gently. At snack time Jomon put a spare biscuit beside Ujjwal's cup and said nothing else.

qa.q: What did Jomon spot at the market?
qa.a: Jomon spotted a jar of orange sweets.

qa.q: How was Jomon's own tantrum at the market different from the way he acted when Ujjwal had one at school?
qa.a: At the market Jomon was the one overwhelmed and needed his father to stay calm and help him breathe, while at school he stepped back, told the teacher and was kind to Ujjwal later at snack time.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he hid his face in his father's shirt?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and sorry, because people were watching after his screaming.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that helped Jomon, and what might have kept the shame stuck?
qa.a: Naveen kept the limit, stayed calm and said it was over, so Jomon could fix things with him; calling Jomon bad would probably have left the shame stuck.

grounding: A young child's own tantrum, the shame afterwards and a friend's tantrum at school show how a calm limit and kind repair differ from fear and stepping back.

passage: The restaurant owner's fourth message of the night said the menu design was "all wrong" and that Suraj had misread the brief, though the brief had changed twice. Suraj's hands shook with anger. He closed the laptop, walked around the block, and in the morning wrote back: the agreed scope in three lines, a note that the new sections would be priced separately, and a polite closing. On the next call the owner talked over Indu, Suraj's junior, and called her slow. Suraj waited until the call ended, then wrote privately that comments about the team should stay about the work, and told Indu in front of the others that her layouts were exactly what had been agreed. Meanwhile the gym owner had asked for a ninth round of free changes, paid the last invoice six weeks late, and kept mentioning big projects next year. Suraj drew up a contract with three milestones and asked for half the fee before starting. When the gym owner declined, he thanked them and ended the engagement, sorry but steady. Santosh's brief arrived on time with photos and colours listed, and the payment came the same afternoon, along with Suraj's name on the launch post. Suraj sent his files early and admitted he could not do animation, suggesting someone who could.

qa.q: How many milestones did Suraj put in the contract?
qa.a: The contract had three milestones.

qa.q: How did Suraj's handling of the gym owner differ from his dealings with Santosh?
qa.a: With the gym owner, who wanted a ninth round of free changes and paid late, he set milestones, asked for half the fee first and politely ended the job; with Santosh, who gave a clear brief and paid on time, he sent files early and was honest about what he could not do.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he closed the laptop after the fourth message?
qa.a: He felt furious and unfairly blamed, since his hands shook, and he stepped away to calm down before replying.

qa.q: What could Suraj do if the restaurant owner is rude to Indu again?
qa.a: He could step in privately again, hold the line on tone, and keep backing Indu openly instead of ignoring it to keep the client happy.

grounding: A freelancer's week with four clients shows scope-changing anger, exploitation, a respectful client, and protecting a junior teammate.

passage: "We took you on as a favour, you know," the supervisor told Irfan in his third week, handing him another stack of files. Irfan nodded and stayed until nine every night, feeling he owed them everything. The work was full days with no stipend, and the promise of a job after the trial had not been repeated. He felt used but did not want to lose the firm's name on his CV. In the next department, Kashish sat with him for an hour over a spreadsheet, gave him a real client summary to draft, and marked his mistakes without sighing. He began arriving early just to hear her explain things. At a wedding, his mother, Vidya, told the aunties that her son worked at a big firm. Irfan smiled and felt a lump in his chest. That night he told her the truth: mostly unpaid, but Kashish was teaching him a lot, and he had a plan. He would ask about a stipend and learning goals, give it until the end of the month, and ask Kashish for a reference either way. "And if nothing changes, I'll leave," he said.

qa.q: How long did Irfan plan to give the firm before deciding?
qa.a: He planned to give it until the end of the month.

qa.q: How did the supervisor's talk of a favour differ from what Kashish did, and how did each shape Irfan's feelings?
qa.a: The supervisor's favour made Irfan feel he owed endless work, so he felt indebted and used, while Kashish taught him properly and gave real tasks, so he admired her and wanted to learn.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when his mother told the aunties about the big firm?
qa.a: He felt a guilty gap, with a lump in his chest, because her pride did not match his unpaid days.

qa.q: What made Irfan's talk with his mother a good next step?
qa.a: He told her the truth gently, said what he was learning and laid out a plan, instead of keeping up the pretence. 🙂

grounding: One intern meets a firm that treats a favour as a debt, unpaid work, a teaching manager and a parent's pride, and reaches an honest plan.

passage: Yamini opened the chatbot and typed, "Explain how monsoon winds form, like I'm in ninth grade." The answer was clear, and she rewrote it in her own words, then asked it to point out mistakes in her maths homework and checked each one herself. Her classmate Indu messaged, "Just make it write the whole history essay. Nobody will know 🙂" Yamini stared at the blank page. The relief sounded lovely, but she remembered last term, when shortcuts left her unable to answer the teacher's question in class, and she remembered the school's rule about doing your own work. She asked the chatbot to quiz her instead. Later it gave her a confident list of three books for her project, and two of them did not exist when she searched the library website and asked the librarian. Her face went hot. At dinner her father, Francis, said, "I read that these tools will take everyone's jobs." Her mother looked worried too. Yamini pulled out her laptop and showed them the quiz, the wrong book list and her notes. "So I check everything," she said. They agreed on a daily time limit and talked about which skills would stay useful.

qa.q: What did Yamini ask the chatbot to do with her maths homework?
qa.a: She asked it to point out mistakes in her maths homework.

qa.q: How did Yamini's use of the chatbot differ from what Indu suggested, and what did the book list show about trusting it?
qa.a: Yamini used it as a helper and did her own thinking, while Indu wanted it to write the whole essay, which skips the learning; the invented books showed that a chatbot can sound sure and still be wrong.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she stared at the blank page after Indu's message?
qa.a: She felt tempted by the easy relief but uneasy, because she remembered what happened last term.

qa.q: How could Yamini's parents support her use of the tool?
qa.a: They could look at how she uses it, keep the daily time limit they agreed on, and keep talking with her about skills that stay useful.

grounding: One teenager uses an AI chatbot as a helper, resists the temptation to have it write her work, catches invented sources and eases her parents' fear.
